chunk_findings.detail: The new conflict message tells the caller to repeat the probe with `ddflow probe {item} --against {against}`, where `against` is the `shown` value. The earlier item-named-`main` fix does not answer this because it only special-cases the literal argument `main`; it does not make the resolved default-branch name safe to pass back through `--against` [r-tell-dont-discover].

chunk_findings.detail: In `probe`, the conflict path returns `O.failed(KIND, data["text"], **data)`, and the unavailable path at the next return does the same with `O.nothing(KIND, data["text"], **data)`. `data` already contains the key `"text"` (`"text": _text(res, item, shown)`), so when the outcome constructors take `text` as their second positional parameter — as the nearby `O.ok(KIND, **data)` path relies on — this passes `text` twice and raises `TypeError: got multiple values for argument 'text'`. Any conflicting pair, or `[locks].probe` off / probe unavailable, therefore crashes instead of returning the documented conflict or unavailable outcome.

chunk_findings.detail: `shown = peer if target == MAIN else target  # the ref actually probed` is wrong when `--against` names another item whose lease branch differs from its item id. `peer = _branch(st, cfg, target)` resolves the branch actually passed to `PR.run`, but `shown` is reset to the item id. For example, peer item `ddflow-43` with lease branch `users/bob/topic` is probed against `users/bob/topic`, but the returned data has `"against": "ddflow-43"` and the conflict text says `Merge ddflow-43 into the branch`, which is not a git ref. The event consumer cannot recover the actual peer branch from `against`; it only has the peer sha in `base`.

chunk_findings.detail: The version parser only keeps major and minor components, so a patch-level minimum is ignored. With `min_git="2.38.1"` and a repository using git 2.38.0, `_tuple(min_git)` is `(2,38)` and `have < (2,38)` is false, so `run` uses `git merge-tree` instead of the documented scratch-merge fallback even though the configured minimum is not satisfied.

chunk_findings.detail: In scratch-merge conflict reporting, the code parses `why` with `_FILES` and `found.group(1).split(",")`. Comma is a valid byte in a git path, so a file named `a,b.txt` is reported as two conflict paths (`a` and `b.txt`) rather than one. The same `_FILES` regex also stops at `;`, truncating a path like `a;b.txt`. The structured conflict object should be used instead of string-splitting on delimiters that can appear in filenames.

chunk_findings.detail: The command documents exit statuses in `summary`/`description` (0 clean, 1 conflict, 2 unavailable), but the declaration contains no exit-code/status mapping: it only sets `cli=CliPolicy(body_always=True)`, and `conflict`/`unavailable` are returned in `payload` as normal results rather than raised errors. Given a conflicting pair, `ddflow probe ITEM --against PEER` will print the conflicting paths and exit 0, so any script relying on the documented exit status 0=clean will treat a conflict as merge-ready, violating the command's own “never read as clean” guarantee.

The suite therefore exercises a second git invocation path that production does not use, so adapter error mapping and timeout behavior can regress while these tests still pass.

chunk_findings.detail: The new conflict message tells the caller to repeat the probe with `ddflow probe {item} --against {against}`, where `against` is the `shown` value. When the request used the magic default-branch target, `shown` is the resolved default-branch name, not the literal `main` that was accepted as input. Because `probe()` resolves `--against` by first checking `target == MAIN` and then `target in st.items`, a default-branch name that is also an item id does not round-trip. Example: repository default branch is `trunk`, and there is an item id `trunk` whose lease branch is `users/alice/trunk`. `ddflow probe ddflow-1` (or `ddflow probe ddflow-1 --against main`) correctly probes against default branch `trunk` and reports a conflict. The returned text then says to re-probe with `ddflow probe ddflow-1 --against trunk`; running that command takes the `trunk in st.items` branch and probes `users/alice/trunk` instead, so an agent or script can see a clean re-probe while the conflict against default branch `trunk` remains. The earlier item-named-`main` fix does not answer this because it only special-cases the literal argument `main`; it does not make the resolved default-branch name safe to pass back through `--against` [r-tell-dont-discover].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/probe.py:_text (conflict re-probe clause)

chunk_findings.detail: The new conflict-path filter `names = tuple(n for n in _both_changed(repo, item, against) if n in said)` treats any raw path that is a substring of the conflict prose as a conflicting path. Given a base containing files `a` and `a,b`, where the item and peer both modify `a` in non-overlapping hunks (so `a` merges cleanly) and both modify `a,b` in the same hunk (so only `a,b` conflicts), `_both_changed` returns both `a` and `a,b`; if `str(why)` contains `conflicting files: a,b;`, the substring test also matches `a`, so the Probe returns `a` as a conflicting path even though it was not conflicted. The fallback should restrict names to the actual conflicted path list, not arbitrary substring membership in the whole `why` text.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/probe.py:_scratch

chunk_findings.detail: The new parser still treats `", "` and `";"` as unescaped structural separators, so legal git paths containing those sequences are misreported. If both sides changed `a`, `b`, and `a, b`, and only `a, b` conflicts, `_both_changed` returns sorted `("a", "a, b", "b")`; for conflict prose `conflicting files: a, b;` `_split_names` matches the prefix `a, ` and parses the remainder as `b`, returning `("a", "b")` instead of the single known path `("a, b",)`. Likewise, with known `("a;b",)` and prose `conflicting files: a;b;`, `_LISTED = re.compile(r"conflicting files: ([^;]*)")` captures only `a`, parse fails, and the probe reports CONFLICT with no paths (`git named no path`) even though a path was named. The recorded paths and the conflict advice are therefore wrong for such inputs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/probe.py:_split_names

chunk_findings.detail: The semicolon half of previous finding #11 is still not answered. `_LISTED = re.compile(r"conflicting files: ([^;]*)")` stops the captured list at the first `;`, so a valid Git path containing a semicolon is silently dropped. With a scratch merge conflict on `a;b` and `_both_changed` returning `("a;b",)`, CI prose such as `conflicting files: a;b; resolve ...` makes `found.group(1)` equal `"a"`, `parse("a")` matches no known path, `_split_names` returns `()`, and `_scratch` returns `Probe(CONFLICT, SCRATCH, (), ...)`. The API then reports CONFLICT with `(git named no path)` even though the conflicting path is known. The new exact-sequence parser fixes comma splitting but not semicolon truncation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/probe.py:101 `_split_names`

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard `if any(";" in n or ", " in n for n in known): return known` runs before the message is parsed, so it returns the both-changed paths even when the message does not contain a `conflicting files:` list. For example, `PR._split_names("no list here", ("a;b",))` now returns `("a;b",)` instead of `()` (the same kind of call the existing test makes with `("a",)`). If `_scratch` uses a non-empty return from this helper as the conflicting paths for a failed scratch merge, a non-conflict scratch failure that happens to have an ambiguous both-changed path is reported as a textual conflict with false paths. The superset fallback should apply only when a conflicting-files list is present/ambiguous, not whenever any known path contains `";"` or `", "`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/probe.py:_split_names

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard is too broad: it returns every `known` path as soon as any known path contains `;` or `, `, without even looking at `said`. Input: `known = ("src/a;b.txt", "src/c.txt")` and `said = "conflicting files: src/c.txt;"` with only `src/c.txt` actually conflicting. `_split_names` returns both paths, so the probe falsely reports the clean `src/a;b.txt` as conflicted. The ambiguity only exists when the separator-bearing path is itself present in the list; when `said` is parseable without it, the exact answer is `("src/c.txt",)`. The same guard also makes `_split_names("no list here", ("a;b",))` return `("a;b",)` instead of the documented `()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/probe.py:_split_names

chunk_findings.detail: The new ambiguity guard still decides by arbitrary substring matching over the whole `said` string, so it can report clean both-changed paths as conflicting. For example, `PR._split_names("conflicting files: src/c.txt; see src/a;b.txt", ("src/a;b.txt", "src/c.txt"))` captures only `src/c.txt` as the `conflicting files:` list (the regex stops at the first `;`), but `odd` is non-empty because `src/a;b.txt` appears in the trailing note, so line 116 returns both paths. The probe then reports `src/a;b.txt` as a conflicting path even though it is not in the parsed conflicting-files list. The same substring rule makes `PR._split_names("conflicting files: a;b;", ("a", "a;b"))` return `("a", "a;b")` when `a` merged cleanly, because `a` is a substring of `a;b`. The fix for the previous overbroad superset guard therefore still overreports: it should restrict odd-name detection and the superset return to the parsed list/token boundaries, not arbitrary prose.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/probe.py:112

chunk_findings.detail: The new `odd` branch returns every known path where `n in said`, not just the separator-bearing paths that are actually listed as conflicts. A clean shorter path can ride along as a substring of a longer conflicted path. Example: `known = ("xa;by", "a;b")`, both sides changed both files, but only `xa;by` conflicts and the scratch message is `"conflicting files: xa;by;"`. Here `"a;b" in said` is true because `xa;by` contains `a;b`, so `_split_names` returns `("xa;by", "a;b")` and the probe falsely reports the clean `a;b` as conflicted even though the prose names only `xa;by`. A boundary-aware match against the listed paths would avoid this false positive.

A wrong but non-UTF8-strict decode such as `b"a\xff".decode("latin-1")` and `b"a\xfe".decode("latin-1")` yields two distinct strings (`"aÿ"` and `"aþ"`), so this test would pass even though the returned paths still are not the exact filesystem names `os.fsdecode`/`surrogateescape` would produce. The added regression test therefore does not actually enforce that non-UTF-8 conflict paths are kept exact, only that they are not collapsed together.
